content.text:
**Ответ: кандидат 1** (оценка в уме; самые близкие соперники — 0 и 2).

**Общие потери.** У всех кандидатов первые дни (0–4) уходят в нехватку: стартового запаса 34 и 52 не хватает до первой поставки в день 5. Здесь планы не различаются.

**Кандидат 6 (заказ каждый день).** Около 25 дней с заказом × 55 ≈ 1375 только фиксированных платежей. Это примерно на 700 больше, чем у планов «через день». Экономия на хранении такую разницу не покрывает.

**Кандидат 3 (заказ раз в 3 дня).** Поставки по 200–240 единиц упираются во вместимость 232. При разбросе спроса излишек пропадает, растут хранение и списания.

**Кандидат 0 и его варианты 4, 5, 7 (заказ через день).**
- Заказ дня 20 (70 + 150) приходит в день 25. Утром там ещё лежат около 29 единиц товара 1. Из 150 единиц товара 1 место находится только для 133, около 17 штук пропадает уже на прогнозных значениях.
- Заказ дня 14 (120 + 88) при приходе в день 19 тоже чуть превышает вместимость: 236 при лимите 232. Кроме того, он тянет большой запас товара 0 через вечера и платит за его хранение.
- У кандидата 7 количества больше, переполнение ещё сильнее. Кандидат 5 чуть меньше, но всё равно переполняется в день 25. Кандидат 4 добавляет к товару 0, переполнение в день 25 остаётся.

**Кандидат 1.** Это кандидат 0, у которого два проблемных заказа разбиты на два дня: день 14 → 43/47 и 91/46 на день 15; день 20 → 29/112 и 46/48 на день 21. Так он попадает под всплески спроса (83 по товару 0 в день 20, 102 по товару 1 в день 25) без переполнения и с меньшим хранением. Это стоит 2 × 55 = 110 фиксированных платежей. Выигрыш — около 150+ на пропавшем товаре плюс 50–70 на хранении, и при случайном спросе запас прочности у него больше.

**Кандидат 2 (заказ через день, по нечётным дням).** Дней с заказом на два меньше, чем у кандидата 1, поэтому он экономит те же 110. Зато уже на прогнозе получает нехватку товара 1 в дни 18–19: примерно 14 единиц × (5 упущенной маржи + 6 неустойки) ≈ 154. Поставка 116 + 95 в день 20 при разбросе спроса тоже близка к переполнению.

I picked **candidate 1**: on forecast values it beats the base plan, candidate 0, by about 200, mainly because it avoids most of the warehouse overflow. I worked this out by hand on average demand, so the gaps between the closest candidates are approximate.

**1. How often to order.** Every order day costs 55 up front.
- **Daily ordering (6):** 25 order days cost 1375, which is 660 more than ordering every two days (715). It saves only about 18.5 a day in storage, roughly 460 over the month, so it comes out behind.
- **Every three days (3):** fixed costs are 220 lower. But storage roughly doubles, adding about 460. Big deliveries also go over the 232 limit, for example on day 11. It is worse than ordering every two days.

**2. Plans that order every two days (0, 1, 4, 5, 7, and 2 with a shift).**
- **Candidate 0:** stock slowly builds up, and the big orders overflow the warehouse. Order 120+88 (day 14) arrives on day 19 and loses about 25 units of product 1. Order 70+150 (day 20) arrives on day 25 and loses about 18 more, which also causes about 10 units of shortage.
- **Candidate 1:** same plan as 0, but each of those two big orders is split over two days (43+47 and 91+46; 29+112 and 46+48). That costs 110 in extra order fees. It removes both overflows and the shortage, and leaves only about 19 units lost on day 27. Overall it gains about 200 over candidate 0.
- **Candidate 7:** the largest quantities. Stock overfills as early as day 11 (about 26 units lost) and keeps building up.
- **Candidate 2:** its deliveries fall on the demand spikes, but the warehouse is already too full when they arrive. About 42 units are lost on day 20 and 25 on day 24, and there is a shortage of about 30 units of product 1 on days 24–25.
- **Candidates 4 and 5:** same timing as 0, with the same big day-14 order. Candidate 4 carries more of product 0 and less of product 1. Candidate 5 is smaller across the board: it overflows less but risks more shortages when demand runs high. Product 1 has the higher shortage cost (11 per unit against 0.4 a night to store), so cutting it is risky. These two are the closest to 1, and I did not simulate them day by day, so this is the least certain part of the comparison.

**3. Randomness.** In both products a missing unit costs about 11, while a spare unit costs only 0.4–0.7 a night to store. So it pays to keep some extra stock, as long as the warehouse doesn't overflow. Candidate 1 does this best, because it splits its large orders so they don't hit the 232 limit.

I'd pick **candidate 2**. I compared them roughly in my head using the forecast demand, not with a full day-by-day simulation of every plan.

**Losses that are the same for every plan.** Nothing ordered can arrive before day 5. Opening stock covers only 34 of the 109 units of product 0 demanded over days 0–4, and 52 of 179 for product 1. So every plan loses the same sales and pays the same penalties at the start, and that doesn't separate them.

**Where plans differ: the 232-unit storage limit at the two demand peaks.** Product 0 has a spike of 83 on day 20, and product 1 has a spike of 102 on day 25.
- **Candidates 0, 4, 5 and 7** order every other day on even days. The peak day lands in a two-day delivery together with the next day. On day 19, 120 + 88 = 208 units arrive, or 225 for candidate 7, on top of leftovers. On day 25, 220 units arrive, plus 20–30 units still left from the day-23 delivery. Space runs out, and product 1, which is unloaded second, is thrown away even though it is the dearer item and already paid for. Candidate 7 orders about 25% above forecast, so its overflow is the worst. Candidate 5 orders about 3% above forecast, which is below the multiplier's average of 1.046, so it also runs short of stock.
- **Candidate 3** delivers every three days, 215–230 units at a time, so it hits the storage limit almost every delivery. It is the weakest plan.
- **Candidate 1** is candidate 0 with the two peak deliveries split across two days. This removes the overflow but adds 2 × 55 = 110 in order fees.
- **Candidate 6** orders every day. It pays 25 × 55 = 1375 in fees, about 550 more than a plan with 13 orders. It saves only about 450 in storage costs, so it loses on balance.

**Candidate 2** places 13 orders, the same as candidate 0. Its deliveries are shifted by one day: each order covers days (6,7), (8,9) and so on. That pairing gives easier peaks:
- the 83 on day 20 is paired with the low 21 on day 21: 116 units ordered against 104 forecast;
- the 102 on day 25 is paired with day 24: 140 units ordered against 142 forecast.

Even at the busiest delivery, about 209 units plus leftovers, the expected overflow is only a few units. It orders about 1.10–1.12 times the forecast for both products. That fits the average demand multiplier of 1.046 and the fact that a lost sale costs more than ordering a spare unit, especially for product 0. With the storage limit rarely reached, the plan also holds up better when demand comes in below the forecast. So it avoids the overflow losses without paying the extra order fees of candidates 1 and 6.

I picked **candidate 4**. This is a rough estimate worked out in my head, not a full day-by-day simulation, so my confidence is moderate.

**How often to order.** Lead time is 5 days and shelf life is 7, so leftovers carry over and overstock is cheap. That makes ordering every other day the best cadence.
- **Candidate 6** orders every day. It pays the 55 fee 25 times instead of 13, about 660 extra. The holding it saves is only around 400–500, so it comes out behind.
- **Candidate 3** orders every three days. Its deliveries are huge (for example 120+110 arriving on day 20) and, together with leftovers, go over the 232-unit capacity, so units are lost on arrival. It also pays more holding.
- **Candidate 2** is the same every-other-day scheme on odd days and should land close to the main group, but nothing in it gives it an edge.

**How much to order.** Candidates 0, 4, 5 and 7 have the same structure and differ only in quantities. The plan doesn't react to what actually sells, so any excess over mean demand (forecast × 1.046) piles up and later spoils. Any shortfall becomes penalties.
- **Product 0:** a missing unit costs 6 in lost margin plus a 5 penalty, 11 in total. An extra unit costs at most about 7 (purchase 4 plus holding). So it pays to order above the mean.
- **Product 1:** a missing unit costs 5 + 6 = 11, and an extra unit also costs about 9 + 2 = 11. So ordering about the mean is right.

**Comparing them** (order size as a share of forecast demand over the two days it covers):
- **Candidate 5** orders about 1.02–1.03×, below the 1.046 mean, so it falls short on both products.
- **Candidate 0** orders about 1.10× on both. That's reasonable for product 0 but a bit high for product 1.
- **Candidate 7** orders about 1.25× on both. Surplus builds up, goods spoil, and it presses against capacity.
- **Candidate 4** orders about 1.2× on product 0 and about 1.05× on product 1. That matches the cost balance above for each product separately, so I expect it to have the highest expected profit.

**Выбор: кандидат 1.** Считал в уме и только примерно, поэтому выбор обоснован, но не доказан.

1. **Начало одинаково у всех.** Первые заказы приходят только в день 5. Стартового запаса (34 и 52) на дни 0–4 не хватает: спрос на товар 0 за эти дни около 109. Неустойка в эти дни у всех кандидатов почти одинаковая и на сравнение не влияет.

2. **Кандидат 3 (заказ раз в 3 дня).** Партии по 216–240 единиц приходят на склад, где уже лежит остаток. Это больше вместимости 232, и излишек пропадает уже оплаченным. Кроме того, такие партии дольше лежат на складе, поэтому хранение дороже.

3. **Кандидат 6 (заказ каждый день).** Склад почти не переполняется, и хранение дешёвое. Но фиксированная плата за 25 заказов равна 25 × 55 = 1375 против 13 × 55 = 715 при заказе через день. Лишние ~660 примерно равны экономии на хранении (~540) или больше её.

4. **Кандидаты 0, 4, 5, 7 (через день, большие партии ко дням пикового спроса).** Это один и тот же план в разном масштабе. Узкое место — заказ дня 20 на 220–230 единиц (у кандидата 4 — 232), он приходит в день 25 (там спрос на товар 1 равен 102). Утром дня 25 на складе ещё ~15 единиц от прошлых партий. Получается 15 + 220 = 235 > 232, то есть часть пропадает даже при прогнозном спросе. При случайном спросе (множитель около ±30 %) переполнение становится частым. В день 19 запас тоже почти впритык: 208 + ~15 = 223. Кандидат 7 закупает больше всех, поэтому переполняется сильнее остальных. Кандидат 5 закупает меньше всех и чаще недопоставляет. Кандидат 4 добавляет товар 0 за счёт товара 1 и тот же риск переполнения не снимает.

5. **Кандидат 2.** Тот же ритм через день, только со сдвигом на нечётные дни. Риски пикового прихода у него слабее (~211 в день 20 и ~209 в день 24), но остаётся заметное переполнение и хранение.

6. **Кандидат 1.** Совпадает с кандидатом 0, кроме двух мест: крупные заказы дней 14 и 20 разделены на два соседних дня. Поэтому склад не переполняется ни в день 20 (пик 83 по товару 0), ни в день 25 (пик 102 по товару 1). Цена — две лишние платы за заказ, всего 110, и это меньше ожидаемых потерь от переполнения и лишнего хранения. Он же устойчивее всех к отклонениям спроса от прогноза.

I'd pick **candidate 7**, though I'm not very confident. I worked this out in my head by rough estimates, not a full day-by-day simulation, and candidates 0, 4 and 7 are close.

1. **Days 0–4 are the same for everyone.** Orders take 5 days to arrive, so every plan runs short on both goods in those days. This doesn't separate the candidates.
2. **Candidate 6 loses on order fees.** It orders on 25 days instead of about 13, which costs roughly 650–700 more in the 55-per-order fee. Its timing is no better than the others', so it can't make that back.
3. **Candidate 1 is candidate 0 with two extra orders.** Splitting two orders costs another 110 in fees for almost no gain in timing.
4. **Candidate 3 orders every 3 days.** That saves about 220 in fees. But each delivery is about 200–230 units, so with what's already in stock it hits the 232-unit limit (for example, about 11 units of good 1 lost on day 11). The third day of each cycle is also more likely to run short when demand is random.
5. **Candidates 0, 4, 5, 7 and 2 order every 2 days**, covering the same delivery days, and differ mainly in how much spare stock they carry:
   - Real demand averages about 4.6% above the forecast, so candidate 5 (about +3% over forecast) actually plans below real demand. Candidates 0 and 2 (about +10%) are only a little above it.
   - Running short costs about 11 per unit for either good (lost margin plus penalty). Ordering too much costs much less: leftovers sell over the next few days, and holding costs only 0.4–0.7 per unit per day. So extra stock is worth it.
   - Rough estimate: with the small spare stock of candidate 0, shortages lose about 1,400. With candidate 7's spare stock of about 20% above real demand, shortage losses fall to about 400, and the extra holding cost is about 450.
6. **Candidate 7's main risk is the warehouse limit.** On days 19 and 25 it receives 225–230 units on top of leftover stock, so it will probably lose some good 1 to overflow, up to several hundred in value. Candidate 2 has smaller peak deliveries (about 210), so it overflows less, but it also carries less spare stock.

Overall, candidate 7's fewer shortages seem to outweigh its overflow losses. Candidate 4 (more spare good 0, slightly less good 1) is a close second.

I'd pick **Candidate 1**, though without much confidence. Everything below is mental arithmetic on the forecast values, and the gap to Candidate 0 is small.

1. **Days 0–4 are the same for everyone.** Orders only start arriving on day 5, and the starting stock (34 and 52) is well short of demand on those days. Every plan pays the same penalties there, so this period doesn't separate them.

2. **Candidate 3 is out first.** It orders every 3 days in batches of about 216–240 units. With leftovers on top, that exceeds the 232-unit capacity, so stock that was already paid for is lost on arrival.

3. **Candidate 6 pays too much in fees.** It orders every day, which costs 25 × 55 = 1375 in order fees against about 715 for the every-other-day plans. The roughly 660 extra isn't covered by smaller peaks.

4. **Candidates 7 and 4 over-order.** They order about 15–20% above the forecast, while real demand averages about 1.046 × forecast. Because the plan is fixed, the surplus builds up each cycle, ends in capacity overflow and spoilage, and has to be paid for.

5. **Candidate 2 overflows on day 24.** The order from day 19 (69 + 140 = 209) arrives then, and about 63 units are still left from the day-22 delivery of 93 + 96. That's about 272 units against a limit of 232. Around 40 units of item 1 are lost, at least 360 in purchase cost alone.

6. **Candidate 0 overflows on day 25.** The order from day 20 (70 + 150 = 220) arrives, and about 29 units of item 1 remain from day 23. That's about 249 units, so roughly 17 units of item 1 are lost, about 150 in cost. The day-19 delivery (120 + 88 = 208) is also close to capacity if demand comes in low.

7. **Candidate 1 is the same plan as 0, with two orders split.** The day 14 and day 20 orders are each split over two days. This adds 110 in fees but spreads out the peak deliveries on days 19–20 and 25–26, so neither goes over capacity. When actual demand varies, this matters more: one low-demand day before a big delivery hurts Candidate 0 much more than Candidate 1.

Candidate 5 is a more cautious version of 0. It has the same peaks and runs short more often. A shortage costs about 11 per unit (lost margin plus penalty), so it's unlikely to come out ahead.

Expected profit is close between 0 and 1. I give the edge to Candidate 1 because it handles random demand better.

Я выбираю **кандидата 4** — он вероятнее всего даёт наибольшую ожидаемую прибыль. Оценка сделана в уме, как требовало задание, и уверенность в ней умеренная, не полная.

**Частота заказов.**
- **Кандидат 6** заказывает почти каждый день: около 25 дней с заказами, это примерно 1375 только фиксированных платежей. Остальные планы с заказом раз в 2 дня платят около 715. Перерасход примерно в 660 он ничем не отыгрывает.
- **Кандидат 3** заказывает раз в 3 дня и экономит около 220 на фиксированных платежах. Но средний запас у него больше, и хранение обходится примерно на 400–450 дороже. Кроме того, партии около 200–216 единиц плюс остатки впритык подходят к лимиту склада в 232. При случайном спросе часть прихода будет пропадать, а дефицит в конце длинного цикла случается чаще.
- **Кандидат 1** — это кандидат 0 с двумя дробленными заказами (дни 14/15 и 20/21). Пики спроса (товар 0 в день 20, товар 1 в день 25) кандидат 0 и так покрывает одним заказом, так что кандидат 1 просто платит лишние 110.

**Запас сверх прогноза среди планов «раз в 2 дня»** (кандидаты 0, 4, 5, 7):
- **Товар 0:** нехватка единицы стоит 6 недополученной маржи плюс 5 неустойки, итого 11. Лишняя единица стоит около 4 плюс хранение и не пропадает сразу, потому что годность 7 дней. Поэтому выгодно держать запас примерно на 15–20 % выше прогноза. Нужно учесть ещё, что средний множитель спроса 1,046.
- **Товар 1:** нехватка тоже стоит около 11, но лишняя единица дороже, около 9. Поэтому выгоднее держаться около 1,05 от прогноза.

| Кандидат | Товар 0 к прогнозу | Товар 1 к прогнозу |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | ≈1,03 | ≈1,02 |
| 0 | ≈1,10 | ≈1,10 |
| 4 | ≈1,2 | ≈1,05 |
| 7 | ≈1,25 | ≈1,25 |

- **Кандидат 5** держит слишком мало и часто будет платить неустойку.
- **Кандидат 0** близок к оптимуму, но по товару 0 держит маловато, а по товару 1 многовато.
- **Кандидат 4** подходит ближе всех к оптимуму по обоим товарам.
- **Кандидат 7** держит слишком много: излишки копятся, растёт хранение, часть товара списывается по сроку годности, а при всплесках спроса есть риск переполнить склад.

I'd pick **Candidate 4**. This is a judgement call from rough mental arithmetic, not a full day-by-day simulation, and Candidates 1 and 0 are close behind.

**What it costs to have too little vs too much.** The main question is how big each order should be compared with the forecast.
- **Good 0:** a missing unit loses its margin of 6 plus a penalty of 5, so 11 in total. A spare unit costs only 0.7 per day to store. It also lasts 7 days, so it can still be sold in the next two-day window. Ordering well above the forecast pays off.
- **Good 1:** a missing unit also costs 11 (margin 5 plus penalty 6). A spare unit costs only 0.4 per day to store, though it costs 9 if it expires or is lost to overflow. Ordering a little above the forecast is enough.
- **Demand runs high:** on average actual demand is about 4.6% above the forecast, so ordering exactly the forecast leaves you short.

**The candidates:**
- **Candidate 6** places an order every day, about 25 order days. At 55 per day that is roughly 660 more in order fees than plans ordering every other day (13 days). That alone makes it the worst.
- **Candidate 3** orders every 3 days, delivering about 216–230 units at once. The warehouse holds 232, so any leftover stock causes overflow. That is a large loss risk.
- **Candidate 7** orders about 25% above the forecast for both goods. Its biggest deliveries are 225 units on day 19 and 230 on day 25, so it will almost certainly overflow, and spare good 1 piles up and expires.
- **Candidate 5** orders almost exactly the forecast (about 1.02–1.03×). Given the higher average demand, it will run short often, at 11 per missing unit.
- **Candidates 0 and 2** order about 10% above the forecast, so good 0 still runs short fairly often. Their peak deliveries are 208–220 units. They are roughly equal, with ordinary overflow risk.
- **Candidate 1** is Candidate 0 with two big orders split in half. That costs 2 × 55 = 110 more in fees but almost removes the overflow risk around days 19–20 and 25, and it brings in more good 0 for the day-20 demand spike.
- **Candidate 4** orders about 20% above the forecast for good 0, which suits its cost balance. For good 1 it orders about 5% above, which is reasonable. Its weak point is day 25: 232 units arrive while about 15–20 units are left over, so some good 1 will overflow. I estimate that at about 150–200, which the extra good 0 sales should more than cover.

**Ranking:** 4 ≳ 1 > 0 ≈ 2 > 5 > 7 > 3 > 6.

I chose **candidate 0** as the most likely best plan, though not with high confidence. The margin over candidates 1 and 4 is small: tens of money units. I worked this out in my head from forecast averages and did not simulate the random demand.

**Fixed cost of order days.** Each day with an order costs 55.
- Ordering every other day (13 order days, about 715) is clearly cheaper than ordering daily. Candidate 6 orders on 25 days, about 1,375, so it pays roughly 660 more.
- Candidate 3 orders every 3 days, which saves on the 55 fees. But each delivery is about 210 units plus leftover stock, so it hits the 232-unit warehouse limit and pays more for storage.

**Size of the orders.** A shortage costs about 11 per unit for either product (lost margin plus the penalty). Leftover stock mostly just costs storage until the next delivery, so ordering a bit above forecast pays off. Candidate 0 orders about 1.05–1.1 times the forecast demand for each 2-day cycle. That roughly matches the average demand multiplier of 1.046 and leaves a small buffer.

**Warehouse overflow on day 25.** The day-20 order arrives on day 25, ahead of the demand spike for product 1 (102). Units that don't fit are lost after being paid for, and product 1 is accepted last, so it is what gets lost.
- Candidate 7: 230 units arrive plus about 36 left over, so about 34 units of product 1 are lost. It also orders 15–25% above forecast throughout, so old stock builds up and expires.
- Candidate 4: 232 units arrive plus about 18 left over, so about 18 units of product 1 are lost (around 160).
- Candidate 0: 220 units arrive plus about 15 left over, so only about 3 units are lost.
- Candidate 5 doesn't overflow, but it orders less across the board, so it runs short more often under random demand.

**Candidate 0 against candidate 1.** Candidate 1 is candidate 0 with the day-14 and day-20 orders each split across two days. That avoids overflow but costs an extra 110 in order fees. Candidate 0's expected overflow loss is about 10 units × 9 = 90, so it comes out slightly ahead.
